<action type="say">
Here’s what to do right now, in order, to limit damage and germs:

1) Pull water back and stop spread
- Use towels/blankets to make a “dam” at the furthest wet part of the hallway.
- Work from the dry area toward the bathroom:
  - Lay towels on wet spots, step/press to soak up water.
  - Wring into the tub, sink, or a bucket and repeat until there’s no standing water.
- If you have a wet/dry shop vac, use it on the worst areas first (bathroom, then hallway).

2) Protect the floor and neighbor below
- Remove bath mats/area rugs from wet areas immediately and hang them over the tub/shower rod so air can reach both sides.
- If any furniture or items with wooden legs are in the wet hallway:
  - Move them to a dry area if you can.
  - If not, put something under the legs (foil, plastic bags, lids, etc.) to keep them off the wet floor.
- Pay extra attention to edges:
  - Press towels firmly along baseboards, at the doorway, and around the toilet base to pull water out of seams where it can drip down.

3) Start active drying (mold prevention)
- Ventilation:
  - Turn on the bathroom fan if you have one.
  - Open windows near the bathroom/hallway if possible.
- Air movement:
  - Aim a fan at the wet areas, blowing from bathroom toward the hallway and, ideally, toward an open doorway or window.
- If you have a dehumidifier:
  - Run it near the bathroom/hallway with doors/windows mostly closed to that zone so it can pull moisture out of the air.
- Plan to keep fans/dehumidifier going for at least 24 hours, longer if the floor still feels cool/damp.

4) Disinfect the area (after most water is up)
Even clear toilet water can carry germs, so disinfect:

- Wear gloves if possible.
- Option A: Bleach solution (if your floor tolerates it and room is well-ventilated)
  - Mix about 1 cup regular bleach in 1 gallon of water.
- Option B: Any household disinfectant/floor cleaner labeled as killing germs (follow the label).
- Use a mop or cloth to:
  - Thoroughly wet all affected hard surfaces in the bathroom and hallway (where water reached).
  - Let it sit for at least 5–10 minutes.
  - Wipe again with clean water afterward if using bleach or if the floor manufacturer recommends it.
- Wipe any splashed baseboards/walls with the same solution, then dry with a clean towel.

5) Check for hidden damp spots
- Run your hand along:
  - Baseboards in and just outside the bathroom.
  - The wall where the hallway got wet.
- If anything feels damp:
  - Keep the fan pointed at those areas.
  - Note exactly where for the plumber and for building maintenance to check behind walls/ceilings if needed.

6) Contact building maintenance (for downstairs ceiling risk)
- Call/message your building’s emergency or maintenance line and say:
  - You had a toilet overflow in your 3rd-floor unit.
  - Water reached about 2–3 feet into the hallway.
  - You’ve shut off the valve and are actively drying and disinfecting.
  - Ask them to inspect the ceiling of the unit below and any walls under the bathroom/hallway.

7) While you wait for the plumber
- Keep that toilet’s shutoff valve closed; don’t use or flush it.
- Keep towels you’ve used either in the tub or in a bag; later, wash them on a hot cycle with detergent (and a little bleach if the fabric allows).
- Keep fans and/or dehumidifier running continuously.

If you tell me what kind of flooring you have in the bathroom and hallway (tile, vinyl, laminate, hardwood, or carpet), I can give you any extra, flooring-specific steps to protect it and reduce risk to your downstairs neighbor.</action>

<action type="say">
Here’s what to do now, tailored to tile (bathroom) and laminate (hallway):

1) Bathroom – tile
- Keep removing water:
  - Use towels or a wet/dry vac to get rid of all visible water.
  - Press towels into grout lines, around the toilet base, and along baseboards to pull water out of joints.
- Disinfect:
  - Tile and grout can handle stronger cleaners.
  - Mix ~1 cup regular bleach in 1 gallon of water OR use a bathroom disinfectant.
  - Mop/wipe all wet tile and grout; let it sit 5–10 minutes.
  - Then go over once with clean water to rinse if you used bleach.
- Dry:
  - Run the bathroom exhaust fan if you have one.
  - Aim a fan at the floor; keep the door open.
  - Try to get grout looking/feeling dry within a few hours.

2) Hallway – laminate
Laminate is vulnerable to swelling if moisture gets into seams.

Right now:
- Pull out as much moisture as possible:
  - Lay towels over every wet area, especially seams between boards and near baseboards.
  - Step/press firmly, then wring into a bucket/tub and repeat until towels are only slightly damp.
- Focus on edges:
  - Work carefully along:
    - The transition strip between tile and laminate.
    - Baseboards and door trim where water reached.
  - Press towels into those corners and gaps; that’s where water can run down toward your neighbor’s ceiling.
- Air movement:
  - Aim a fan low across the laminate, blowing along the wet area.
  - Keep it running continuously for at least 24 hours (longer if the floor still feels cool/damp to the touch).

Disinfecting laminate (toilet water concern):
- Don’t soak it—no mopping with lots of liquid.
- Use a disinfectant that’s safe for laminate/hard floors:
  - Lightly spray onto a cloth or lightly onto the floor—avoid puddles, especially in seams.
  - Wipe all the areas that were wet.
  - Let it sit for the contact time on the label (often 5–10 minutes).
  - Immediately follow with a dry towel to remove extra moisture from the surface and seams.
- Wipe baseboards where water touched with the same disinfectant on a cloth, then dry.

3) Mold and downstairs-neighbor risk – what to watch
Next 24–48 hours:
- On your laminate:
  - Check if boards start to:
    - Lift at the edges (cupping),
    - Bubble,
    - Feel soft/spongy when stepped on.
  - If you see this, mention it to maintenance; those sections may need to be replaced.
- Walls/baseboards:
  - Feel for any cool/damp spots along the baseboards where water traveled; keep the fan aimed there if you find any.
- For the downstairs unit:
  - You already saw no ceiling leak below right now, but still inform building maintenance that:
    - Toilet overflow on 3rd floor,
    - Water reached 2–3 feet into laminate hallway,
    - You’ve soaked up water, disinfected, and are running fans.
  - Ask them to check the ceiling below your bathroom/hallway in case moisture shows up later.

4) When the plumber/maintenance arrives
Tell them:
- Where water reached: tile bathroom floor and 2–3 feet into laminate hallway.
- What you’ve done: shut off valve, removed standing water, disinfected, and are actively drying with fans.
Ask them to:
- Check under/behind the toilet and around the wax ring for leaks or damage.
- Advise whether any laminate needs to be lifted or if they want to open small inspection areas to ensure things are dry.

If you can roughly estimate how many “planks” of laminate got wet and whether they still look perfectly flat vs. slightly lifted, I can help you gauge how likely long-term damage is and how pushy to be with building maintenance.</action>
